To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a variable fraction (up to 50 %) of sequence reads in 16S amplicon surveys of low-density samples is derived from exogenous DNA (reagent contaminants and cross contamination of negative controls) and that the fraction of exogenous DNA in a sample can be estimated by qPCR targeting the 16S V3 region and that a decontamination procedure can be used to remove contaminating sequences from the dataset.

a significant fraction of 16S amplicon sequence reads originate from exogenous DNA and that these contaminant sequences can be removed from 16S amplication sequence datasets using a decontamination pipeline that combines OTU abundance with bacterial DNA quantitation by qPCR.

a variable fraction (0.01–0.5%) of 16S amplicon sequence reads in datasets from low-density microbiota and diluted mock communities originated from exogenous sources and that the fraction of exogenous DNA in a sample can be estimated by qPCR and used for in silico removal.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the removal of contaminant sequences in low-density microbiota samples and the development of a pipeline that combines the relative abundance and bacterial load of operational taxonomic unit sequences.
the removal of contaminant sequences from 16S rDNAs datasets.
the identification of unexpected taxa and their removal from microbiota surveys.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the described decontamination procedure is not suitable for the removal of contaminant DNA sequences from negative extraction controls.
the described decontamination procedure is not suitable for removal of contaminant sequences in negative extraction control samples.
decontamination of amplicon datasets by the described procedure is not recommended.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the described pipeline can be used as a tool to identify unexpected OTUs in 16S amplicon datasets.
we developed a pipeline that is able to detect and remove contaminants from low density microbiome samples.

the described pipeline for decontamination is useful to remove contaminants in low biomass samples, such as those obtained from environmental samples, but it should be used with care in samples with a high biomass, such as those from human samples.
The main takeaway from our work is that
qPCR is an efficient method for the identification of reagent contaminants in microbiota samples, and that this information can be used for in silico removal from the 16S amplicon sequence dataset.
the use of qPCR to quantify bacterial DNA in a sample is a useful tool to improve the quality of 16S amplicon sequence data.
the presence of reagent contaminant sequences in low-density microbiota datasets is a major problem and should be addressed by the research community.
